meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine singular demonstrative (هاي مدرسة الروابي، هاي أول مرة).

examples.trans: This is my friend Dina.
This idea is excellent.

meanings.note: Central setting: مدرسة الروابي للبنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls').

examples.trans: The school is close to our house.
I like going to school early.

meanings.note: Singular بنت, definite البنت, plural بنات / البنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls' = مدرسة الروابي للبنات).

examples.trans: She is a very bright girl.
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Invariable Levantine relative pronoun replacing الذي / التي / الذين and 'what' (اللي صار 'what happened').

examples.trans: The girl whom I saw is my friend.
Tell me what happened.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.

examples.trans: I didn't hear the bell.
Come before the school closes.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine indefinite person word; ما حدا means 'nobody'.

examples.trans: Is anyone in the classroom?
Nobody believed me.

meanings.note: Literally 'play', and idiomatically ما حدا بيلعب معها / معي ('nobody messes with her / me').

examples.trans: We played ball in the courtyard.
Don't play this game with me.

meanings.note: Takes suffixes معي (with me), معك (with you), معها (with her), معنا (with us), معكم (with you all), معهم (with them), and forms مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!').

examples.trans: Come sit with us.
Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

meanings.note: Plural صحبات is the everyday Jordanian word for girlfriends / school friends (صحباتي، صحباتها).

examples.trans: Dina is my closest friend.
I sat with my friends in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine pronunciation (daayman) of classical دائماً.

examples.trans: She always comes early.
We always sit here.

meanings.note: Construes with عن for the person defended (بيدافعوا عنها 'they defend her').

examples.trans: Her friends always defend her.
I defended myself in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: Marks topics (عني 'about me'), distance (ابعدي عن طريقي 'away from my path'), and defense (بيدافعوا عنها 'defend her').

examples.trans: We talked about the movie yesterday.
Stay away from her, please.

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.

examples.trans: Come here, Mariam.
Thank you very much, Miss.

meanings.note: Appears in the dramatic warning يا ويل البنت اللي... ('woe to the girl who... / heaven help the girl who...').

examples.text: يا ويل اللي بيتأخر عن الحصة.
examples.trans: Woe to whoever is late to class.
We're in trouble if the teacher heard us.

meanings.note: Used in بتوقف بطريقها ('stands in her way') and كيف بتوقفي بوجهي ('how dare you stand in my face').

examples.trans: She stood by me during the trouble.
The bus stopped in front of the school.

meanings.note: Used literally and figuratively: بطريقها ('in her way') and ابعدي عن طريقي ('step out of my way').

examples.trans: Step out of my way, please.
The way to school is short.

meanings.note: Invariable modal word: introduces polite requests (ممكن أعرف؟ 'may I know?', ممكن تضبي... 'could you...') and possibility (ممكن تخسر 'might lose').

examples.trans: May I ask you a question?
Anything could happen.

meanings.note: In the past مع ما (ما عرفت شو أعمل), means 'I didn't know what to do'; b-present بعرف means 'I know'.

examples.trans: I know this place well.
I didn't know how to answer the question.

meanings.note: Independent first-person singular pronoun for any gender.

examples.trans: I am a student at the school.
I didn't say anything.

meanings.note: Quintessential Levantine 'why?' (literally 'for what thing?': لـ + إيش).

examples.trans: Why were you late today?
I don't know why she got upset.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian/Levantine word for 'here' (formal هنا).

examples.trans: Come sit here next to me.
Life is very sweet here.

meanings.note: Standard Jordanian private-school address for a female teacher or principal, used alone (يا مس) or before her first name (مس فاتن، مس عبير).

examples.trans: Yes Miss, I'm ready.
Ms. Faten is in her office now.

meanings.note: Spoken feminine singular 'you', spelled with final ي to reflect the Jordanian pronunciation inti.

examples.trans: Are you a new girl here?
What do you think?

meanings.note: Active participle of عرف, regularly used instead of the present tense for current awareness (إنتي عارفة منيح).

examples.trans: I know the whole story.
I didn't know about the appointment.

meanings.note: Core Levantine word (mniih) used adverbially after verbs of knowing or listening: عارفة منيح ('know very well'), اسمعي منيح ('listen well').

examples.trans: Listen to me well, Noaf.
I know the story well.

meanings.note: Ms. Faten says ليش ناديتك ('why I called/summoned you to my office').

examples.trans: The teacher called my name in class.
I called you, but you didn't hear me.

meanings.note: Asks about manner or state (كيف كان الفيلم؟ 'how was the movie?', شفت كيف... 'I saw how...').

examples.trans: How are you today?
How did you get here?

meanings.note: Used in Jordanian speech with subjunctive forms like أأذيها ('hurt her') and يأذوا ('they hurt').

examples.trans: I didn't mean to hurt you.
They won't hurt anyone.

meanings.note: Used by teachers and students for a female classmate (زميلتك بالصف).

examples.trans: She is my classmate in the same class.
Respect your classmates at school.

meanings.note: High-frequency Jordanian word for 'like': زي هيك ('like this') and زي هاد المكان ('like this place').

examples.trans: There is nobody like you.
Do like we agreed.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine manner word: ليش بتحكي هيك؟ ('why are you talking like that?'), زي هيك ('like this'), بعد هيك ('after this').

examples.trans: Don't talk to me like that.
That's not what we agreed on.

meanings.note: Negates nouns, adjectives, participles, prepositional phrases, and لازم (مش صح، مش معنا، مش قادرة، مش بعد اليوم).

examples.trans: This talk is not true.
I'm not upset with you.

meanings.note: Active participle of قدر; أنا مش قادرة أستوعب means 'I am unable to take in / process'.

examples.trans: I can't believe the news.
You are definitely able to succeed.

meanings.note: Often paired with مش قادرة ('I can't wrap my head around what happened').

examples.trans: I can't process the news.
Did you grasp the whole lesson?

meanings.note: Two essential senses: 'happen' (اللي صار 'what happened') and 'become / turn into' (صارت كابوس، صار الوقت).

examples.trans: Tell me what happened exactly.
It's time we head to class.

meanings.note: Takes the person asked directly (اسألي البنت، سألتك سؤال).

examples.trans: I want to ask you a simple question.
Ask the teacher about the homework.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine verb for 'find': البنت اللي لقتها ('the girl who found her').

examples.trans: I found my notebook in the classroom.
Where did you find the key?

meanings.note: With بـ + الـ, بالصدفة means 'by coincidence / by chance'.

examples.trans: We bumped into each other in the courtyard by chance.
I found out the news by coincidence.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'do' or 'make' (بعمل وظيفة 'doing homework', بعملوا مشاكل 'making trouble').

examples.trans: How did you do on the exam?
I didn't do anything wrong.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine dative base taking pronoun endings: إلي (to me), إلك (to you), إلها (to her), إلنا (for us), إلهم (to them).

examples.trans: This book is for you.
Tell me the truth.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, أي asks 'which?' (أي موضوع؟) or strengthens negation ('not any' -> أي إشي).

examples.trans: Which class are you in?
I didn't make any mistake.

meanings.note: Signature Jordanian/Palestinian word corresponding to formal شيء; definite form الإشي, plural أشياء.

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
Nothing happened.

meanings.note: Versatile Levantine word meaning 'but' between clauses and 'only / just' inside a clause.
As a focus adverb before a verb, noun, or imperative, بس narrows or softens the statement.

examples.trans: I tried to speak, but she didn't hear me.
I just want one minute.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, كل means 'every' (كل يوم، كل إشي); with الـ (الكل) it means 'everyone'; with suffixes (كلنا، كلهم، كلها) 'all of us/them/it'.

examples.trans: Everyone knows the story.
We see each other every day.

meanings.note: Primary spoken verb for 'see' across the Levant, also used in farewells like أشوفك بكرة! ('See you tomorrow!') and نشوفك! ('See you!').

examples.trans: I saw everything with my own eyes.
See you tomorrow morning!

meanings.note: Idiomatic in شفت بعيني / بعينها ('saw with my/her own eyes') and بتشوفه العين ('the eye sees').

examples.trans: I saw what happened with my own eyes.

examples.text: مش كل إشي بتشوفه العين صح.
examples.trans: Not everything the eye sees is true.

meanings.note: Besides 'he/it', separates a definite subject from a definite predicate to mean 'is' (مش كل إشي بتشوفه العين هو الحقيقة).

examples.trans: Honesty is the most important thing.
Where is the notebook?

meanings.note: Definite الحقيقة refers to what actually happened behind appearances.

examples.trans: Everyone must know the truth.
The truth will come out soon.

meanings.note: Appears in المرة الجاي ('next time'), أول وآخر مرة ('first and last time'), بالمرة ('at all'), and plural مرات ('sometimes').

examples.trans: This is the first time I come here.
Sometimes we sit in the library.

meanings.note: البنت القوية refers to the seemingly untouchable popular girl at school.

examples.trans: Stay strong, Mariam.
Her voice is strong and clear.

meanings.note: Used in تخسر كل إشي ('lose everything').

examples.trans: I don't want to lose my friends.
She could lose everything in a moment.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'tomorrow' (أشوفك بكرة! 'See you tomorrow!').

examples.trans: We have an exam tomorrow morning.
See you tomorrow at school!
